Intelligence / Supply Chain & Process
AI & Agentic AI in Supply Chain & Process

Your supply chain should fix itself before you notice it broke.

Agentic AI turns forecasting, replenishment, and exception handling into a self-correcting system instead of a set of dashboards someone has to watch.

A single delayed vessel at Jebel Ali or a demand spike in one distribution zone can cascade into stockouts, expedited freight costs, and margin erosion across an entire GCC network within days. Most supply chain teams still react to these events manually — checking dashboards, calling suppliers, re-keying data across ERP, WMS, and TMS systems that don't talk to each other. Agentic AI closes that gap by continuously monitoring, deciding, and acting within guardrails you set, so disruptions get absorbed before they reach the customer.

How It Works

Five ways agentic AI shows up in supply chain & process.

01

Demand forecasting agents

Agents blend POS data, seasonal patterns (Ramadan, back-to-school, summer slowdowns), and external signals like weather or event calendars to produce SKU-level forecasts that update daily rather than monthly, catching demand shifts before they become stockouts.

02

Autonomous replenishment triggers

Rather than waiting for a planner to review reorder reports, agents generate and route purchase orders automatically when inventory crosses dynamic thresholds, factoring in lead times, MOQs, and supplier reliability history.

03

Cross-system exception handling

Agents watch ERP, WMS, and TMS systems simultaneously, catching mismatches — a shipment marked delivered in the TMS but not received in the WMS — and resolving or escalating them before they distort inventory records.

04

Supplier risk monitoring

Agents track supplier performance, customs clearance patterns, and news signals affecting key trade lanes (Red Sea disruptions, port congestion at Jebel Ali or Jeddah Islamic Port), flagging at-risk orders early enough to trigger backup sourcing.

05

Real-time inventory rebalancing

When one distribution node runs high and another runs low, agents propose or execute inter-warehouse transfers automatically, weighing transfer cost against stockout risk rather than leaving the imbalance for a weekly cycle count to surface.

Illustrative Example

The scenario below is a composite, illustrative example built from patterns Neural Horizons AI sees across supply chain & process engagements in the region — not a specific named client, and figures are illustrative rather than audited results.

A regional FMCG distributor operating across the UAE and Saudi Arabia

The challenge: The organization was losing sales to recurring stockouts in fast-moving categories while simultaneously carrying excess inventory in slower regional depots, with planners unable to reconcile signals across three disconnected systems fast enough to act.

The approach: Neural Horizons AI deployed a network of forecasting, replenishment, and exception-handling agents integrated directly into the client's existing ERP and WMS, with human approval required above defined order-value thresholds.
